title: The Guru is the Granth
hook: after the Ardas many recite the couplet: by the Timeless One's command the panth was founded, and all Sikhs are to accept the Granth as Guru

segments.voice: Yesterday: chardi kala, and your line: rising spirits, good for all. Today, what many Sikhs say in the moment right after that line.

The Ardas is over. Everyone has bowed. In many gurdwaras, before anyone sits, a few more lines ring out, sung or chanted, often by the whole hall at once. They aren't a prayer, exactly. They're closer to a reminder, said aloud, of who is in charge here. And who is in charge is right there at the front of the room, under a canopy, wrapped in cloth: a book. The scripture itself.
screen: `THE ARDAS IS OVER.` → `A FEW MORE LINES RING OUT.` → `WHO IS IN CHARGE HERE?`

segments.voice: The couplet goes, in its best-known form: aagiaa bhai akaal ki, tabhi chalaayo panth. By the command of the Timeless One, the panth, the Sikh community, was set on its way. Sabh sikhan ko hukam hai, guru maaniyo granth. All Sikhs are commanded: accept the Granth as Guru. It often continues: accept the Guru Granth as the visible body of the Gurus, and whoever wishes to meet the Lord, seek in the Shabad, the Word. Here's the history it remembers. In 1708, at Nanded in the Deccan, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, was near death. Sikh tradition says that instead of naming an eleventh human Guru, he placed the line of Gurus in the scripture, the Adi Granth, from then on called Guru Granth Sahib. Spiritual authority went to the Word; the Khalsa panth would carry it in the world. The couplet itself isn't from the Guru Granth Sahib. It's a later verse of the Sikh tradition, and historians discuss exactly when it took this form. But the idea it states is the center of Sikh practice. That's why, in a gurdwara, the Granth sits higher than anyone, why people bow before it, why it's put to rest at night and opened again at dawn. The respect isn't for paper and ink. It's for the voice of the Gurus that Sikhs hear in those pages. So guru maaniyo granth isn't a slogan. It says where to look: for Sikhs, to seek the Guru is to open the Word.
screen: `BY THE TIMELESS ONE'S COMMAND.` · `1708: GURU GOBIND SINGH AT NANDED.` · `THE LINE OF GURUS PASSES TO THE WORD.` · `SEEK THE LORD IN THE SHABAD.` · then, large: `GURU MANEYO GRANTH.`

segments.voice: If you're in a gurdwara, you can bow before the Guru Granth Sahib the way the congregation does; if not, sit quietly and let your head lower a little, slowly, the way you'd nod to a teacher you respect. Notice what it feels like to bow to wisdom rather than to someone's power, and rest there, breathing, as if waiting for a teacher to speak. If you pray, say Waheguru once as your head comes up.
Nanded, where in 1708 Guru Gobind Singh placed the Guru's authority in the scripture: Sikhs call it Guru Granth Sahib, and seek the Guru in its Word.
Your line: guru maneyo granth. Ten Gurus, and then the Word, from Nanded on. That's day six hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: After the Ardas, many congregations recite the dohra aagiaa bhai akaal ki… guru maaniyo granth, then bow before the Guru Granth Sahib and raise the jaikara.

chat.says: Why was there no eleventh human Guru after Guru Gobind Singh?
options: Tradition says at Nanded he placed the Guruship in the scripture; Sikhs accept the Granth as Guru.
The Khalsa held a vote and decided to stop choosing Gurus once the tenth one died.
He named the Akal Takht itself as the eleventh Guru, to rule over all Sikhs.
